messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 63
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Publisher
  trauma_type: Man-made disaster
  pcl5: 79

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Dream Residue: Waking up from a nightmare, Event Recall: Talking about the event, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Friends: avoid seeing friends, Sit With Back to Wall: always sit with back against a wall to see the room, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled
  Memory: Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Thomas is a sixty-three-year-old publisher who, for the past several years, has been living inside a waking nightmare he cannot shake. He is a large man, broad-shouldered, with the kind of steady, deliberate presence that served him well in boardrooms and at editorial meetings. But now, that steadiness is gone. He comes to the clinic at his wife’s urging, though he would never call it that—he says he is here because he cannot keep going like this, and because his marriage is beginning to fray under the weight of what he cannot control.

The event that changed everything happened three years ago, when he was attending an industry conference in a high-rise hotel. A gas leak in the building’s kitchen caused an explosion that tore through the ballroom during a cocktail reception. Thomas was standing near the bar when the blast threw him against a wall, shattering his glasses and filling his lungs with smoke and the acrid, sweet smell of alcohol and burnt wiring. He crawled through debris, past overturned tables and people who were not moving, until he found an exit. He was not physically injured beyond cuts and bruises, but something inside him broke that night. He has not been the same since.

The memory of that moment is not a story he tells; it is a series of pictures that appear in his mind without warning, as vivid as the moment they were taken. He sees the chandelier swinging, the carpet peeling up in waves, the look on a woman’s face as she pressed a napkin to her bleeding arm. These images are not fuzzy or faded with time—they are sharp, detailed, and they arrive when he does not want them. The worst times are when he wakes from a nightmare, still half-caught in the dream, and the images linger like a film over his actual bedroom. He lies there, heart pounding, unable to tell for a moment whether the smell of smoke is real or remembered.

The smell of alcohol is a particular torment. He cannot walk past a bar or stand near someone drinking a beer without the olfactory memory yanking him back into that ballroom. At dinner parties, he has started to excuse himself before the wine is poured. At home, his wife has stopped having a glass of wine in the evenings, because she cannot bear the way he flinches when she brings it near him. He knows this is unfair, but he cannot help it. The smell is a trigger he cannot avoid, and so he avoids the people who might bring it into his space.

He has stopped seeing friends. Not all at once, but gradually, over months. Each invitation became a calculation: will there be alcohol? Will someone ask about the conference? He started declining, then stopped returning calls. His wife goes to social events alone now, and the silence between them when she comes home is heavy with things neither of them says. He knows she is lonely. He knows he is the reason. But the thought of sitting in a room full of people, of being asked a casual question about his work, of having to talk about the event or even hear someone else mention a similar story—it feels impossible. The memory forces its way into his mind when he is least prepared, and he has learned that the only way to keep it at bay is to keep his world small.

At work, he has become a different man. Once known for his calm, collaborative style, he now insists on sitting with his back to a wall in every meeting. He scans the room constantly—checking exits, watching who enters, noting where people are standing. His colleagues have noticed; they think he has become paranoid or controlling. He cannot explain to them that he is not looking for a better angle on the quarterly report—he is looking for the nearest way out. Even in his own home, he feels on guard. He jumps at ordinary sounds: the furnace kicking on, a car door slamming outside, the creak of the staircase. His wife has learned to announce herself before entering a room, because she once found him standing in the kitchen, white-knuckled, after she dropped a spoon.

He is exhausted. The hypervigilance does not switch off. He startles at sounds that would not bother most people—the hiss of a coffee machine, the clatter of a delivery truck—and each time, his body floods with adrenaline as if the explosion is happening again. He has come to believe that he is broken, that something fundamental in him was shattered in that ballroom and cannot be repaired. What frightens him most, he says, is not the memories themselves, but the feeling that he is losing himself. He does not recognize the man who cannot sit in a restaurant, who avoids old friends, who lies awake at night trying not to dream. He came to therapy because his wife told him she could not watch him disappear anymore. And he came because, somewhere underneath the fear, he is still the man who used to believe he could fix things. He hopes that might still be true.
